message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
**No, the line shouldn't run as written.** The central claim is wrong. Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria, so they do nothing against flu and won't help anyone get back to work sooner. NHS and international health guidance is clear on this.

Publishing it could also cause real harm:
- It encourages staff to ask GPs for drugs that won't help.
- Unnecessary antibiotics can cause side effects such as stomach upset and allergic reactions, and they contribute to antibiotic resistance.
- "As any doctor will tell you" puts a false claim in doctors' mouths.

## Why his GP may have prescribed them

There are legitimate reasons, but none of them make the column's advice right. Doctors sometimes prescribe antibiotics when flu leads to a **secondary bacterial infection**, such as a chest infection or pneumonia, or when they suspect one. That is different from antibiotics treating flu itself. There are also **antiviral** medicines for flu, which are prescribed mainly for people at higher risk of complications. People sometimes remember these as "antibiotics".

## A suggested replacement

> **If you come down with flu:** rest, keep warm and drink plenty of fluids. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease fever and aches. Please stay at home while you have symptoms so it doesn't spread around the office. Antibiotics don't work against flu, because it's a virus. But do contact your GP or NHS 111 if your symptoms are severe or getting worse, if you're short of breath, or if you're in a higher-risk group. The best protection is the annual flu jab. Check whether you're eligible for a free one, or whether the company is offering vaccinations this winter.

## Raising it with the facilities manager

You could frame it as an editorial check:

> "We run health tips past the official guidance before publishing, and the NHS is clear that antibiotics don't work on flu, since it's a virus. Antibiotics are sometimes given when flu leads to a chest infection, which might be what your GP was treating. I've suggested a reworded tip that keeps your practical advice."

That corrects the claim without suggesting he was careless. Most of his column's intent, which is helping colleagues recover and stay well, survives the rewrite.
